1.subject: Historical Reliability
1.title: Historical Reliability Of the Bible
1.summary:
A professor calls the Gospels "legends" because they were written decades after Jesus… then holds up his favorite biography of Alexander the Great as "real history."

One student checked the dates. 👀

🏛️ Alexander the Great died in 323 BC. Our earliest surviving history of him (Diodorus) came nearly 300 years later, and the one historians trust most (Arrian) came 400+ years later.
✝️ Paul's letters were written within 20–30 years of the cross, quoting a resurrection creed many scholars date to within a few years of the events. Mark followed within about 40 years, and all four Gospels within a single lifetime, while eyewitnesses were still alive.

If 400 years is good enough for Alexander… 40 is good enough for Jesus.

Would you hold both books to the same standard? Tell me below 👇
1.script:
A professor told his class the Gospels can't be trusted. Too late, he said. Written decades after Jesus died. Basically legends.

Then he held up his favorite book: a biography of Alexander the Great. He tapped the cover. "This is real history."

Alexander died in 323 BC. And the whole lecture hall nodded along.

One student raised her hand. "Sir, when was that written?" He laughed. "Doesn't matter." And the class laughed with him.

That night, she checked.

The earliest surviving history of Alexander was written nearly three hundred years after he died. The one historians trust most, by Arrian, came more than four hundred years later.

Now, Jesus. Paul's letters were written within twenty to thirty years of the cross. He even quotes a resurrection creed many scholars date to within a few years. Mark's Gospel follows within about forty years. All four, within one lifetime.

You see, that early, the eyewitnesses were still alive. Fishermen. Neighbors. Enemies. Invent a miracle, and someone would stand up and say: that never happened.

Next morning, she put both books on his desk. Four hundred years. Forty.

If four hundred years is good enough for Alexander... forty is good enough for Jesus.

2.subject: Manuscript Integrity
2.title: Why The Bible Is Accurately Translated
2.summary:
A TV host lines up ten people to prove the Bible is just a game of telephone. "Jesus rose from the dead" comes out the other end as "Cheese grows on a red bed." 😂

Then a stagehand asks to try it her way…

Telephone only works with ONE line, one whisper at a time, and no way to check the original. But the New Testament spread in every direction at once, to Egypt, Syria, Rome and Greece, copied by different hands in different lands.

📜 Today scholars have over 5,000 Greek manuscripts of the New Testament, some fragments within a century or two of the originals.
🔍 Line them up and the copying slips (spelling, swapped words) stand out and cancel each other out.
📖 Modern Bibles aren't translated English → Latin → German. They go straight back to the Greek.

His game had one line. The Bible has thousands.

Did you think the Bible was a game of telephone? Comment below 👇
2.script:
A TV host lined up ten people to prove the Bible is just a game of telephone.

He whispered, "Jesus rose from the dead." By the tenth person, it came out: "Cheese grows on a red bed."

The audience howled. "Two thousand years of whispers," he said. "That's your Bible."

Then a stagehand raised her hand. "Can I try it my way?" He laughed and handed her the mic.

She split the room into five separate lines. Same message, whispered down all five at once.

Every line garbled something. But never the same thing. Put the five endings side by side, and the original sentence falls right out.

You see, telephone only works with one line, one whisper at a time, and no way to check. The New Testament spread in every direction at once. Egypt. Syria. Rome. Greece. Copies in different hands, in different lands.

Today scholars hold over five thousand Greek manuscripts. Some fragments date within a century or two of the originals. Line them up, and the slips stand out. Spelling. Swapped words. They cancel each other out.

And modern Bibles don't go English to Latin to German. They go straight back to the Greek.

The host looked at her five lines. Then at his one.

His game had one line. The Bible has thousands.

further_reading.text: textual criticism of the New Testament
the Greek manuscript tradition (papyri, uncials, minuscules)

3.subject: The Resurrection
3.title: Nobody Dies for a Lie They Invented
3.summary:
A Roman magistrate brags he can make any liar confess before sundown. A counterfeiter takes one look at the whip and spills everything. 💰

Then they drag in a group of fishermen who claim their executed teacher is ALIVE: that they touched him and ate breakfast with him on the shore.

"Fanatics," he smirks. "People die for crazy beliefs all the time."

But there's a difference:
🔥 A fanatic dies for something someone else told him. He sincerely believes it.
👁️ The apostles weren't repeating a rumor. They claimed they saw it with their own eyes. If it was a lie, they'd KNOW, because they'd be the ones who made it up.

Offered freedom if they'd just say "it never happened," they were beaten, jailed… and sang in their chains.
⚔️ James, by the sword. Peter, in Rome. James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in Jerusalem. Not one of them is ever recorded taking it back.

People will die for a lie they believe. Nobody dies for a lie they invented.

Could you hold out if you knew it was a lie? 👇
3.fiction_note: (The magistrate is a fictional character representing the Roman authorities.)
3.script:
A Roman magistrate bragged he could make any liar confess before sundown.

He'd seen it a hundred times. A counterfeiter took one look at the whip and spilled everything. The guards laughed. "Liars lie for money," he said. "For power. The moment it costs them, they fold."

Then they dragged in a group of fishermen.

Their crime? They kept saying their executed teacher was alive. That they'd touched him. Eaten breakfast with him on the shore.

The magistrate smirked. "Fanatics. People die for crazy beliefs all the time."

You see, there's a difference.

A fanatic dies for something someone else told him. He sincerely believes it.

These men weren't repeating a rumor. They claimed they saw it with their own eyes. If it was a lie, they'd know it. Because they'd be the ones who made it up.

So he offered the deal every liar takes. "Just say it never happened, and you walk free."

They were beaten. Jailed. And that night, in chains, they sang.

James, by the sword. Peter, in Rome. James, the brother of Jesus, stoned in Jerusalem. Not one of them is ever recorded taking it back.

The magistrate stared at his list of confessions. Every name on it had cracked. Except these.

People will die for a lie they believe.

Nobody dies for a lie they invented.

4.subject: Psychological Transformation
4.title: Evidence that Jesus Has Indeed Resurrected
4.summary:
A psychiatrist closes the case in five seconds: "Grief hallucination. Next." 🗂️

His intern isn't so sure, so he opens the file.

Friday night, the disciples are finished:
🐓 Peter, the boldest of them, denies even knowing Jesus. Three times. The first time, to a servant girl.
🏃 The rest scatter.
🔒 They lock themselves in a room, terrified they're next.

Fifty days later, those same men walk into the public square of Jerusalem, the city that had just executed their teacher, and announce he's alive. Thousands hear it, a short walk from the tomb.
⚖️ Arrested, Peter tells the very council that condemned Jesus: "We must obey God rather than men."
🩸 They're flogged, and they keep preaching.

Grief visions are real, but they're private: one mind, one moment, comfort in your own room.
👥 They don't appear to eleven men at once, or to five hundred.
🐟 They don't eat fish.
🚪 And they don't march frightened men out the door to face the people who killed their friend.

Something happened in Jerusalem that broke their fear.

Grief makes mourners. Not martyrs.

What do you think turned them around? 👇
4.fiction_note: (The psychiatrist and the intern are fictional characters.)
4.script:
A psychiatrist closed the case in five seconds. "Grief hallucination. Next."

His intern wasn't so sure. He opened the file.

Friday night. Peter, the boldest disciple, denied even knowing Jesus. Three times. The first time, to a servant girl. The rest scattered. Then they locked themselves in a room, terrified they were next.

Defeated. Hiding. Done.

Fifty days later, those same men walked into the public square of Jerusalem, the city that executed their teacher, and announced he was alive. Thousands heard it. Right there, a short walk from the tomb.

Arrested, Peter stood before the very council that condemned Jesus and said: we must obey God rather than you. Flogged. They kept preaching.

The psychiatrist shrugged. "Grief does strange things."

You see, grief visions are real. But they're private. One mind, one moment, comfort in your own room. They don't appear to eleven men at once. Or to five hundred. They don't eat fish. And they don't march frightened men out the door to face the people who killed their friend.

Something happened in Jerusalem that broke their fear.

The intern slid the file back. "Grief makes mourners. Not martyrs."

The psychiatrist looked at the clock. Then at the file. And for once, he didn't say next.

5.subject: Historical Evidence
5.title: Did Jesus Really Die on the Cross?
5.summary:
A podcaster with two million followers says Jesus never died: "He fainted on the cross. Woke up in a cool tomb. Walked out. Easy." 🎙️

Then a night-shift nurse calls in. "You've never met a Roman execution squad."

⚔️ These men killed for a living, and a guard who lost a prisoner could pay with his own life.
✅ They didn't guess. They checked. Jesus was already dead, so they didn't bother breaking his legs.
🗡️ One soldier drove a spear into his side anyway, and out came blood and water.
📜 Even Pilate double-checked with the centurion before he'd release the body.

"Blood and water? That's poetry," says the podcaster.

But John had no idea what that meant, and doctors do. 🫀 Severe shock and trauma can make fluid collect around the heart and lungs. Pierce the side and you'd expect blood, then a clear, watery fluid. John wasn't writing poetry. He was describing a corpse.

And even if Jesus had somehow survived (shredded back, pierced hands and feet, a hole in his side), a half-dead man doesn't convince anyone he's conquered death.

Romans didn't do "almost dead." And almost dead doesn't start a church.

Have you heard the swoon theory before? 👇
5.fiction_note: (The podcaster and the nurse are fictional characters.)
5.script:
A podcaster with two million followers said Jesus never died. "He fainted on the cross," he laughed. "Woke up in a cool tomb. Walked out. Easy."

A night-shift nurse called in. "You've never met a Roman execution squad."

These men killed for a living. And a guard who lost a prisoner could pay with his own life.

So when they reached Jesus, they didn't guess. They checked. He was already dead, so they didn't bother breaking his legs. One soldier drove a spear into his side anyway, and out came blood and water.

Even the governor double-checked. Pilate questioned the officer in charge before he'd release the body.

The podcaster rolled his eyes. "Blood and water? That's poetry."

You see, John had no idea what that meant. But doctors do. Severe shock makes fluid pool around the heart and lungs. Pierce the side, and out comes blood, then something clear, like water. John wasn't writing poetry. He was describing a corpse.

And even if he'd survived? Shredded back. Pierced hands and feet. A hole in his side. A half-dead man doesn't convince anyone he conquered death.

"Romans didn't do almost dead," she said. "And almost dead doesn't start a church."

For the first time in two hundred episodes: dead air.

further_reading.text: Edwards, Gabel & Hosmer, "On the Physical Death of Jesus Christ," JAMA (1986)
D. F. Strauss, A New Life of Jesus (1864)

6.subject: Eyewitness Testimony
6.title: Name One Witness To Jesus Resurrection
6.summary:
A defense attorney leans back and smirks: "Five hundred witnesses? Name one. No independent witnesses. Case dismissed." ⚖️

Then the court clerk raises her hand. "Your Honor, can I read something?"

📜 Around AD 55, Paul wrote a letter to the church in Corinth listing who saw Jesus alive after his execution: Peter, the Twelve, more than five hundred people at once, then James, Jesus's own brother, who hadn't believed in him.

"Easy to say," laughs the attorney. "Anyone can invent a crowd."

But Paul added one tiny detail: most of them are still alive (1 Corinthians 15:6).
⏳ Not "once upon a time." Still alive, right now.
📣 The letter was read aloud in a city full of skeptics.
⛵ Anyone could sail east, knock on doors, grill the witnesses and compare their stories.
🧱 If even a handful said "never happened," the whole thing would collapse.

Liars hide their witnesses. Paul handed out the guest list.

Would you name 500 witnesses if you were making it up? 👇
6.fiction_note: (The attorney and the clerk are fictional characters. The queue around the courthouse is a visual metaphor.)
6.script:
A defense attorney leaned back in his chair and smirked. "Five hundred witnesses? Name one. No independent witnesses. Case dismissed." The jury nodded.

The court clerk raised her hand. "Your Honor, can I read something?"

Around 55 AD, a man named Paul wrote a letter to the church in Corinth. In it, he listed the people who saw Jesus alive after his execution. Peter. The twelve. Then more than five hundred people, all at once. Then James, his own skeptical brother, who hadn't believed in him.

The attorney laughed. "Easy to say. Anyone can invent a crowd."

You see, Paul added one tiny detail. Most of them, he wrote, are still alive. Not once upon a time. Still alive. Right now.

That's not poetry. That's a dare. This letter was read out loud in a city full of skeptics. Anyone could get on a ship, sail east, and start knocking on doors. Ask them. Grill them. Compare their stories. If even a handful said "never happened," the whole thing collapses.

Liars hide their witnesses. Paul handed out the guest list.

The clerk set the letter down. "You asked where they were. He told everyone."

The attorney looked at the jury. The jury looked at the door. Someone was knocking.

Outside, the line went all the way around the block.

further_reading.text: Gary Habermas & Michael Licona, The Case for the Resurrection of Jesus (2004)

7.subject: Archaeological Grounding
7.title: The Gospel Is True History Not Merely Fictional Stories
7.summary:
A literature professor tosses the Gospels onto his pile of fairy tales: "Same genre. Myths. Once upon a time, in a land far, far away." 🐉

A muddy archaeology student in the back row raises her trowel: "Which page?"

He opens Luke chapter 3: "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod ruled Galilee, and Annas and Caiaphas were high priests…" Then he stops reading.

Fairy tales don't give you coordinates. This does: five rulers, an exact year, real places. Every detail could be checked, and critics doubted several of them for a long time. Then the shovels came out:
🪨 1961: a stone at Caesarea with Pontius Pilate's name and title carved into it
⚱️ 1990: an ornate bone box (ossuary) inscribed with the name Caiaphas
🏛️ The Pool of Bethesda, excavated right where John put it, colonnades and all (John 5:2)
🚧 2004: the Pool of Siloam, found by a crew repairing a sewer pipe (John 9:7)

Dragons never leave fossils. Wizards never leave receipts. But Pilate left a stone.

What archaeological find surprised you most? 👇
7.fiction_note: (The professor and the student are fictional characters.)
7.script:
A literature professor tossed the Gospels onto his pile of fairy tales. "Same genre," he said. "Myths. Once upon a time, in a land far, far away."

In the back row, a muddy archaeology student raised her trowel. "Which page?"

He opened Luke, chapter three. "In the fifteenth year of the reign of Tiberius Caesar, when Pontius Pilate was governor of Judea, Herod ruled Galilee, and Annas and Caiaphas were high priests..."

He stopped reading. The room went quiet.

"Fine," he shrugged. "So they borrowed a few real names."

You see, fairy tales don't give you coordinates. This does. Five rulers. Not once upon a time, an exact year. Real places. Every detail could be checked. And critics doubted several of them for a very long time.

Then the shovels came out.

A stone in Caesarea with Pilate's name carved into it.
A bone box inscribed with the name Caiaphas.
The pool of Bethesda, exactly where John put it, porticoes and all.
The pool of Siloam, found in 2004 by a crew fixing a sewer pipe.

Dragons never leave fossils. Wizards never leave receipts. But Pilate left a stone.

The student dropped a dusty photo on his desk. "Your fairy tale has a dig schedule."

The professor slowly moved the Gospels to a different shelf. The one marked history.

further_reading.text: Craig Blomberg, The Historical Reliability of the Gospels

8.subject: Biblical Harmonization
8.title: Four Witnesses, Four Different Stories
8.summary:
A slick lawyer waves the Gospels at the jury: "They can't even count the angels!" 😇 Matthew has one angel sitting on the stone. Mark has a young man inside. Luke has two men standing. John has two angels sitting. "Somebody made this up."

On the witness stand, an old detective sips his coffee ☕ and tells him about last week's fender bender at Fifth and Main. Four witnesses. One saw the driver's face, one got the license plate, one only noticed the dog, and one was buying a hot dog. 🌭

"You know what I do when four stories match word for word? I go looking for whoever wrote the script."

Identical testimony means somebody rehearsed. Real witnesses stand on different corners. And look at what all four Gospels agree on:
🌅 Early on the first day of the week (Matthew 28:1 · Mark 16:2 · Luke 24:1 · John 20:1)
👣 Women find the tomb first
🙋‍♀️ Mary Magdalene is named in every account
🪨 The stone is rolled away
⚰️ The body is gone

The angel details? Matthew 28:2 · Mark 16:5 · Luke 24:4 · John 20:12. If there were two angels, there was at least one. The details wobble. The core never moves. And if you were inventing a religion, you'd fix the angel count before publishing.

Fake stories match. Real witnesses don't.

Which Gospel detail do you think shows an eyewitness angle best? 👇
8.fiction_note: (The lawyer, the detective and the witnesses are fictional characters.)
8.script:
Four witnesses. Four different stories. The lawyer grinned at the jury. "They can't even count the angels!"

He waved the Gospels. "Matthew: one angel, sitting on the stone. Mark: a young man, inside. Luke: two men, standing. John: two angels, sitting. Somebody made this up."

On the witness stand, an old detective sipped his coffee. "Last week. Fender bender. Fifth and Main. Four witnesses."

One saw the driver's face. One got the license plate. One only noticed the dog. One was buying a hot dog.

"Four different stories," the detective said. "You know what I do when four stories match word for word?"

The lawyer blinked. Twice.

"I go looking for whoever wrote the script."

You see, identical testimony means somebody rehearsed. Real witnesses stand on different corners.

Now look at what all four Gospels agree on. Early on the first day of the week. Women find the tomb first. Mary Magdalene is in every account. The stone is rolled away. The body is gone.

The details wobble. The core never moves.

And if you were inventing a religion, you would fix the angel count before publishing.

The detective set down his cup. "Two angels? Then there was at least one."

The jury nodded. The lawyer sat down.

Fake stories match. Real witnesses don't.

further_reading.text: Simon Greenleaf, The Testimony of the Evangelists (1846)
Craig Blomberg, The Historical Reliability of the Gospels

9.subject: Moral Relativism
9.title: Whatever The Majority Decides Is Right
9.summary:
A professor tells his class that morality is just a vote: "Whatever the majority decides is right." 🎓

A quiet student raises her hand. "Can we test that?" She holds up a cardboard ballot box. "Motion: the professor's car now belongs to the class." 🚗 Forty hands go up. One doesn't. "Motion carries," she says, and dangles his keys.

"That's theft!" "Says who? We voted."

You see, in 1945 men sat in a courtroom in Nuremberg, and their defense was simple:
⚖️ "We broke no German law."
🪖 "We followed orders."
🏛️ "Our nation decided."

The judges didn't answer, "Well, that's your culture." The tribunal's charter defined crimes against humanity as crimes "whether or not in violation of the domestic law of the country where perpetrated." In other words, there is a law above every law.

If morality is just a vote, those judges were wrong, and Germany simply had different preferences. If they had won the war, no one could ever call it evil. Just different.

🏖️ Rights written by a vote are written in sand. The next tide takes them.

Nobody actually lives like that. Not even professors. Especially when it's their car. 🔑

What's one thing you believe would be wrong even if 99% of people voted for it? 👇
9.fiction_note: (The professor and the student are fictional characters.)
9.script:
A professor told his class that morality is just a vote. "Whatever the majority decides is right. That's all right and wrong ever were."

A quiet student raised her hand. "Can we test that?"

He smirked. "Please."

She held up a cardboard ballot box. "Motion: the professor's car now belongs to the class."

Forty hands went up. One didn't.

"Motion carries," she said, and dangled his keys.

"That's theft!" he shouted.

"Says who? We voted."

The room went very quiet.

You see, in 1945, men sat in a courtroom in Nuremberg. Their defense? We broke no German law. We followed orders. Our nation decided.

The judges didn't say, "Well, that's your culture." They called it crimes against humanity, whether or not it was legal at home. A law above every law.

But if morality is just a vote, the judges were wrong. Germany simply had different preferences. And if they had won the war, no one could ever call it evil. Just different.

Rights written by a vote are written in sand. The next tide takes them.

Nobody lives like that. Not even professors. Especially when it's their car.

She tossed back the keys. "Turns out some things aren't up for a vote."

He caught them. And for the first time all semester, he took notes.

further_reading.text: Charter of the International Military Tribunal (1945), Art. 6(c)
Robert H. Jackson's opening statement at Nuremberg (1945)
Paul Copan, "True for You, But Not for Me"

10.subject: Divine Lawgiver
10.title: There Is a Higher Law
10.summary:
A city councilman cuts the ribbon on a new civil rights museum. "We don't need God to know what's right," he tells the cameras. "We have laws." 🎤

The old night guard clears his throat. "In 1963, segregation was the law."

He leads him to a jail cell exhibit. On the bunk lies a newspaper, its margins crammed with handwriting. 📰

✍️ April 1963: Martin Luther King Jr. sits in a Birmingham jail.
⛪ Eight local clergymen publish a statement calling the demonstrations "unwise and untimely." Wait for the courts. Respect law and order.
📝 King begins his reply in the margins of that newspaper: the Letter from Birmingham Jail.
📜 "There are two types of laws: just and unjust… I would agree with St. Augustine that 'an unjust law is no law at all.'"
⚖️ "A just law is a man-made code that squares with the moral law or the law of God."

Take that away, and Alabama's segregation laws were just… the laws. Legally passed. Enforced by police. Nothing higher to appeal to.

"So the law isn't the top," the councilman says quietly.
"Never was."

Human rights need a court above the courthouse. 🏛️

Can human rights exist without something higher than government? 👇
10.fiction_note: (The councilman and the night guard are fictional characters. Dr. King is not depicted.)
10.script:
A city councilman cut the ribbon on a brand-new civil rights museum. "We don't need God to know what's right," he told the cameras. "We have laws."

The old night guard cleared his throat. "In 1963, segregation was the law."

The councilman's smile froze.

The guard led him to a jail cell. On the bunk lay a newspaper, its margins crammed with handwriting.

In April 1963, Martin Luther King Jr. sat in a Birmingham jail. Eight local clergymen published a letter calling his protests unwise and untimely. Wait for the courts, they said. Respect law and order.

He began his answer in the margins of that newspaper. There are two kinds of laws, he wrote. Just and unjust. And with Augustine: an unjust law is no law at all.

You see, how do you tell the difference? King said it plainly. A just law squares with the moral law, the law of God.

Take that away, and Alabama's laws were just... the laws. Legally passed. Enforced by police. Nothing higher to appeal to.

The councilman read the margins twice.

"So the law isn't the top," he said quietly.

"Never was," said the guard. "That's how they knew they were right."

Human rights need a court above the courthouse.

The councilman walked back to the microphone. And crossed out his speech.

further_reading.text: Martin Luther King Jr., "Letter from Birmingham Jail" (April 16, 1963)
"A Call for Unity" (statement by eight Alabama clergymen, April 12, 1963)
Augustine, On Free Choice of the Will, Book I
Thomas Aquinas, Summa Theologiae I–II, Q. 95–96

11.subject: Moral Ontology
11.title: Can You Keep the Fruit and Cut the Roots
11.summary:
An influencer films himself in an apple orchard: "Kindness. Equality. Every human has dignity. No God required. It's just natural." 🍎📱

The old orchard keeper leans on his shovel. "Natural? Says who?"
"Everybody knows that."
"Everybody didn't."

📜 In Roman Egypt (1 BC), a worker named Hilarion wrote to his pregnant wife: "If it is a boy, keep it; if it is a girl, cast it out." The letter was dug out of an ancient rubbish heap at Oxyrhynchus (P.Oxy. 744).
⛰️ In Sparta, Plutarch says, elders inspected every newborn, and the weak were left to die in a ravine at the foot of Mount Taygetus. Nature favors the strong.
🏮 Then a strange group started picking those abandoned babies up and taking them home: Christians. Every child, they said, bears the image of God.
⚖️ By 374, Roman law under Emperor Valentinian had made killing an infant a crime.

Even Nietzsche, who despised Christianity, admitted it. Give up the Christian faith, and you lose the right to Christian morality (Twilight of the Idols, 1888).

Equality. Compassion. Dignity for the weak. Those apples grew on a tree. You can cut the roots, and the apples will hang there a while. 🪚

Where do you think human equality comes from? 👇
11.fiction_note: (The influencer and the orchard keeper are fictional characters.)
11.script:
An influencer filmed himself in an apple orchard. "Kindness. Equality. Every human has dignity," he said, biting an apple. "No God required. It's just natural."

The old orchard keeper leaned on his shovel. "Natural? Says who?"

"Everybody knows that."

"Everybody didn't."

In Roman Egypt, a worker named Hilarion wrote to his pregnant wife. If it's a boy, keep it. If it's a girl, throw it out. Archaeologists dug that letter out of an ancient trash heap.

Abandoning unwanted babies was normal. In Sparta, says Plutarch, elders inspected every newborn. The weak ones were left to die in a ravine. Nature favors the strong.

Then a strange group started picking those babies up and taking them home. Christians. Every child, they said, bears the image of God. By 374, Roman law had banned killing infants.

You see, even Nietzsche, who despised Christianity, admitted it. Give up the Christian faith, and you lose the right to Christian morality.

Equality. Compassion. Dignity for the weak. Those apples grew on a tree.

The keeper held out a saw. "Go ahead. Cut the roots. The apples will hang there a while."

The influencer looked at the apple in his hand.

Then he stopped recording.

further_reading.text: Friedrich Nietzsche, Twilight of the Idols, "Skirmishes of an Untimely Man" §5
Rodney Stark, The Rise of Christianity

12.subject: Human Worth
12.title: Human Worth
12.summary:
A science-show host pours a human being into six jars: water, carbon, calcium, a pinch of iron. "That's you. Total value? About five bucks." 🧪 The crowd laughs. "No soul. No Creator. Just chemistry that got lucky."

An old custodian leans on his mop. "Then where do your rights come from?"
"Evolution. Obviously."
"Funny. A rock has no rights. A puddle has no dignity. Why would a lucky puddle?" 🪨

📜 History has run this math before. Aristotle called a slave "a living tool" (Nicomachean Ethics 8.11).
🏛️ Ancient markets priced people by the head, and buyers inspected them like livestock.
⛪ Then, around 379 AD, Bishop Gregory of Nyssa stood up in church and asked the slave owners: "How many obols did you reckon the image of God was worth?" It is one of history's first voices against slavery itself.
⚖️ Chemistry can add up your atoms. It can't add up your worth. Pile every coin on Earth on one side of the scale. A person made in God's image still outweighs it.

The custodian slides five dollars across the counter. "I'll take you, then."
"I'm not for sale!"
"Then you're not five bucks. And neither is anyone else." 💵

If humans are only atoms, where does human worth come from? 👇
12.fiction_note: (The science-show host and the custodian are fictional characters.)
12.script:
He poured a human being into six jars. Water. Carbon. Calcium. A pinch of iron. "That's you," the science host told the crowd. "Total value? About five bucks."
Everyone laughed. "No soul. No Creator. Just chemistry that got lucky." He even rang it up on a brass cash register.
In the aisle, an old custodian leaned on his mop. "Then where do your rights come from?"
"Evolution," the host said. "Obviously."
"Funny," said the custodian. "A rock has no rights. A puddle has no dignity. Why would a lucky puddle?"
History has run this math before. Aristotle called a slave "a living tool." Markets priced people by the head. Buyers checked their teeth like horses.
Then, in the year 379, a bishop named Gregory stood up in a crowded church and asked the slave owners, "How many coins did you pay for the image of God?" It's one of history's first voices against slavery itself.
You see, chemistry can add up your atoms. It can't add up your worth. Pile every coin on Earth on one side of the scale. A person made in God's image still outweighs it.
The custodian slid five dollars over. "I'll take you, then."
The host stepped back. "I'm not for sale!"
"Then you're not five bucks," said the custodian. "And neither is anyone else."

further_reading.text: Gregory of Nyssa, Homilies on Ecclesiastes, Homily 4
Kyle Harper, Slavery in the Late Roman World

13.subject: Social Contracts
13.title: Is Morality Just a Contract We All Signed
13.summary:
The HOA president bangs his gavel and tapes a contract to the wall. "Morality is just a deal. We all agree not to hurt each other. Society signs it. Done." 📜

In the front row, an old stonemason pulls a string with a weight on the end out of her pocket.
"So whatever the contract says is right?"
"By definition."

History has signed some contracts:
🏛️ 1787: America's founding contract counted each enslaved person as three fifths and promised to return anyone who escaped.
📕 1935: Germany's Reich Citizenship Law stripped Jewish citizens of their citizenship.
🚉 Apartheid South Africa made Black citizens carry passbooks just to move through their own country.
Every one of them was legal. Signed. Stamped. Agreed. Enforced by the police.

"Well, those were wrong."
"Wrong by which contract?"

📏 You can't check a wall with the wall. A mason hangs a plumb line from above. The string doesn't lean with the bricks, and that's how you find the crooked ones. Every contract needs a standard above it.

Then she slides a paper across the table: "New clause. Your house now belongs to the association. Everyone signed."
"That's not right!"
"Exactly. Some things are wrong even when everybody signs." ✍️

If morality is only an agreement, how could a whole society ever be wrong? 👇
13.fiction_note: (The HOA president and the stonemason are fictional characters.)

14.subject: Moral Duty
14.title: Can You Call Evil Evil Without a Rulebook
14.summary:
A TV host smiles into the camera as a lion drags off a zebra. "Nature has no rules. No God. No good. No evil. Just survival." 🦁

His sound intern raises her microphone.
"So nothing out here is ever wrong?"
"Wrong is a human invention."

Out here:
🦁 Lions steal each other's kills, and a new male who takes over a pride kills the cubs that aren't his.
🐣 A cuckoo chick hatches and shoves the other eggs out of the nest.
🐒 At Gombe in the 1970s, one chimpanzee community hunted down a rival group's males, one by one.
Nobody calls it murder. Nobody holds a trial. It's just nature.

🔥 That night he reads the news by the fire: about 27 million people are in forced labor.
"That's evil. Somebody ought to stop it."
And he's right. He's a decent man, and he means it.
"Ought? Says who? The lions?"

⚽ A referee can only blow the whistle if there's a rulebook. No rulebook, no fouls. Just players. The moment you call something evil, you're holding a rule from above the game.

Then a baboon snatches his sandwich.
"Hey! That's stealing!"
"No. That's survival."
"…Fine. It's wrong."
"Exactly. You can't blow the whistle and burn the rulebook." 📕

Where do you think the word "ought" comes from? 👇
14.fiction_note: (The TV host and the sound intern are fictional characters.)
14.script:
Brock smiled into the camera as a lion dragged off a zebra. "Nature," the TV host announced, "has no rules. No God. No good. No evil. Just survival."
Behind him, his sound intern raised her microphone.
"So nothing out here is ever wrong?"
"Wrong is a human invention."
Out here, lions steal each other's kills. A new male takes over a pride and kills the cubs that aren't his. A cuckoo chick hatches and shoves the other eggs out of the nest. At Gombe, chimpanzees hunted down a rival group's males, one by one.
Nobody calls it murder. Nobody holds a trial. It's just nature.
That night, Brock read the news by the fire. Twenty-seven million people in forced labor. "That's evil," he said. "Somebody ought to stop it."
And he's right. Brock is a decent man, and he means it. But the intern looked up. "Ought? Says who? The lions?"
You see, a referee can only blow the whistle if there's a rulebook. No rulebook, no fouls. Just players. The moment you call something evil, you're holding a rule from above the game.
Then a baboon snatched Brock's sandwich.
"Hey! That's stealing!"
"No," she said. "That's survival."
Brock sighed. "Fine. It's wrong."
"Exactly. You can't blow the whistle and burn the rulebook."

further_reading.text: ILO, Walk Free & IOM, Global Estimates of Modern Slavery (2022)

15.subject: Cosmic Fine-Tuning
15.title: Four Royal Flushes in a Row Is Just Luck
15.summary:
Vince lays down his cards. A royal flush. His fourth in a row. The whole riverboat goes quiet. 🃏

"Relax. It's just luck. Play enough card games, and somebody has to get this hand. Infinite games, infinite chances."
The old dealer stops shuffling. "So it's not cheating?"
"It's math."

Nobody buys it. When the odds are that impossible, design is screaming at you.

Now look up:
💥 Hawking: one second after the Big Bang, if the expansion rate had been smaller by one part in a hundred thousand million million (a hundred quadrillion), the universe would have collapsed back on itself.
🌌 A little faster, and no galaxies would ever form.
⭐ Nudge gravity or the strong nuclear force, and you get no stable stars, no carbon, no us.

🫧 Some say there must be infinite universes, and we just got the lucky one.
⚙️ But that only moves the question back. A machine that spits out universes needs its own settings dialed in perfectly. Somebody still built the shuffler.

The dealer flips open Vince's card shuffler. Inside is a tiny switch, set to ROYAL.
"That switch could've just happened."
"Then you've got a lot more faith than I do." 😏

If four royal flushes make you suspect a rigged deck, what should a fine-tuned universe make you suspect? 👇
15.fiction_note: (Vince and the dealer are fictional characters.)
15.script:

The whole riverboat went quiet.

Across the table, the old dealer stopped shuffling.
"So it's not cheating?"
"It's math."
Nobody bought it. They grabbed their money and called him a cheat. Because when the odds are that impossible, design is screaming at you.
Now look up. One second after the Big Bang, if the expansion rate had been smaller by one part in a hundred quadrillion, the universe would have collapsed back on itself. A little faster, and no galaxies would ever form. Nudge gravity, or the strong nuclear force, and you get no stable stars, no carbon, no us.
So some say there must be infinite universes, and we just got the lucky one.
You see, that only moves the question back. A machine that spits out universes needs its own settings dialed in perfectly. Somebody still built the shuffler.
The dealer flipped open Vince's card shuffler. Inside was a tiny switch, set to royal.
Vince swallowed. "That switch could've just happened."
She smiled. "Then you've got a lot more faith than I do."

further_reading.text: Stephen Hawking, A Brief History of Time (1988), ch. 8
Luke Barnes & Geraint Lewis, A Fortunate Universe (2016)
Robin Collins, "The Teleological Argument" in The Blackwell Companion to Natural Theology (2009)

16.subject: Cosmology
16.title: Can a Universe Pop Out of Nothing
16.summary:
The Great Zandor taps his empty top hat. "Science says the universe popped into existence out of nothing. And tonight, so will this rabbit." 🎩🐇

The crowd roars. Then a little girl in the front row raises her hand. "Was the hat really empty?"
"Completely."
She climbs onto the stage and flips the hat over. A false bottom. A trapdoor. And under the stage, a tunnel packed with rabbits.

🌊 That's what physicists mean by "nothing." The quantum vacuum isn't nothing. It's a sea of fluctuating energy, inside space, governed by mathematical laws. It's a hat with a trapdoor.
🕳️ Real nothing means no space. No time. No energy. No laws. Not even a hat. And out of nothing, nothing comes.
🌌 The best evidence in cosmology says space, time, and matter all had a beginning. Even an inflating multiverse would need one (the Borde–Guth–Vilenkin theorem).
✨ If space and time began, whatever started them can't be made of space or time. It has to be timeless, spaceless, immaterial, and unimaginably powerful. And since nothing forced it, it chose.

Zandor snatches the rabbit back. "Fine. But somebody had to put the rabbits there."
"Exactly. Rabbits don't come from nothing. And neither do universes." 🐇

If the universe began, what do you think started it? 👇
16.fiction_note: (Zandor and the girl are fictional characters.)

17.subject: Origin of Life
17.title: Can a Junk Pile Build Itself Into a Truck
17.summary:
Rex aims his camera at a pile of junk. "Folks, give this pile enough time, and it'll build itself into a working truck. Engine, wheels, radio. Billions of years. Pure chance." 🛻

Old Mabel the mechanic wipes her hands on a rag. "And what's going to tighten the bolts?"
"Time, Mabel. Time does everything."

⏳ So they let the camera roll. Days. Winters. Decades. The pile never became a truck. It rusted. It cracked. It crumbled. Time doesn't build things. Time tears them down.

Life has the same problem:
🧪 In 1859, Louis Pasteur put sterile broth in swan-necked flasks. Nothing grew. Some of those flasks are reported to still be clear today. Every experiment since says the same thing: life comes from life.
⚡ In 1953, the Miller–Urey experiment did cook up amino acids. But bricks aren't a building.
🧬 Even the simplest living cell runs on coded instructions (DNA), read by tiny machines (ribosomes) that build other machines, and even proofread their own mistakes (DNA repair). That's not a pile of parts. That's a factory with a library.

Rex stares at the heap of rust. "Okay. So how long would it take?"
Mabel slams the hood of a shiny pickup. "One afternoon. If you've got a mechanic." 🔧

What do you think it would take to get the first living cell? 👇
17.script:
Rex aimed his camera at a pile of junk. "Folks, give this pile enough time, and it'll build itself into a working truck. Engine, wheels, radio. Billions of years. Pure chance."
His followers loved it. Behind him, old Mabel the mechanic wiped her hands on a rag.
"And what's going to tighten the bolts?"
"Time, Mabel. Time does everything."
So they let the camera roll. Days. Winters. Decades. The pile never became a truck. It rusted. It cracked. It crumbled. Time doesn't build things. Time tears them down. Rust always wins.
Life has the same problem. In 1859, Louis Pasteur put sterile broth in swan-necked flasks. Nothing grew. Some of those flasks are still clear today. Every experiment since says the same thing: life comes from life.
In 1953, a famous experiment did cook up amino acids. But bricks aren't a building.
You see, even the simplest living cell runs on coded instructions, read by tiny machines that build other machines, and even proofread their own mistakes. That's not a pile of parts. That's a factory with a library.
Rex stared at the heap of rust. "Okay. So how long would it take?"
Mabel slammed the hood of a shiny pickup. "One afternoon," she said. "If you've got a mechanic."

further_reading.text: Louis Pasteur, "Mémoire sur les corpuscules organisés qui existent dans l'atmosphère" (1861)
Stanley Miller, "A Production of Amino Acids Under Possible Primitive Earth Conditions," Science 117 (1953)
Stephen Meyer, Signature in the Cell (2009)
James Tour, lectures on the origin of life

18.subject: DNA & Information
18.title: Can Spilled Cereal Write You a Note
18.summary:
Derek's cereal spills across the counter, and the letters spell: "Derek, clean your room by five." 🥣
He laughs. "Classic. Gravity, momentum, random bounces. It's just chemistry doing what chemistry does."
His little sister Pip doesn't even look up from her toast. "Cool. Then spill it again."

🔁 So he does. Once. Ten times. A hundred. He gets X, Q. He gets G, R, B, L. He gets cereal in his hair. Not one single word. Letters don't arrange themselves into messages. Messages come from minds.

Now look inside any cell in your body:
🧬 Coiled inside is DNA, over three billion letters long (the human genome has about 3.1 billion base pairs), written in a four-letter code: A, T, C, G.
📖 Read in order, those letters spell out instructions for proteins, for tiny molecular machines, for eyes, for you.
🧪 Chemistry explains the ink, but it doesn't explain the message. The bases can bond along the strand in any order, the same way cereal can land in any order. The order is the information.
📡 And every code whose origin we actually know (Morse code, sheet music, software, cereal on a counter) came from a mind.

Derek looks at the counter. Then at the cell. "So... someone wrote both."
Pip points upstairs. "And it's almost five." ⏰

Can you think of a code that we know wrote itself? 👇

Now open any cell in your body. Coiled inside is DNA, over three billion letters long, written in a four-letter code. A, T, C, G. Read in order, they spell out instructions for proteins, for tiny machines, for eyes, for you.
You see, chemistry explains the ink. It doesn't explain the message. DNA letters can bond in any order, just like cereal can land in any order. The order is the information.
And every code whose origin we actually know, Morse code, sheet music, software, cereal on a counter, came from a mind.

Pip pointed upstairs. "And it's almost five."

19.subject: The Problem of Evil
19.title: What If God Froze Every Evil Act
19.summary:
Gideon holds up a little silver remote. "Ladies and gentlemen, the Guardian. Anyone about to do something evil? Frozen. Instantly. If God really loved us, He'd have built this." 🧊

The town cheers. Somebody even bakes him a cake. In the back row, old Rosa, the school bus driver, raises her hand: "Where do you set it?"
"At evil, Rosa. Obviously."

So they switch it on:
🦹 A mugger reaches for a purse. Frozen. The crowd roars.
🍪 A boy reaches for a second cookie. Frozen.
🐟 A man starts lying about the size of his fish. Frozen.
🗣️ Two ladies lean in to gossip. Frozen.
🌅 By sunset, the whole town stands perfectly still. No crime. No noise. Not one smile.
Gideon smirks. "See? No more evil. These people are idi—" Frozen.

You see, there's no clean line between stopping a murder and stopping all of us. To remove every evil choice, God would have to freeze our fists, then our tongues, then our thoughts. He'd have to remove the chooser.
❤️ And a world where nobody can choose evil is a world where nobody can choose love either. Just a town full of very polite statues.

Rosa squeezes a talking doll. "I love you," it squeaks.
Then she switches off the Guardian, and Gideon's daughter runs and hugs him.
"Feel the difference?"

Would you trade your freedom for a world with no evil at all? 👇
19.fiction_note: (Gideon, Rosa and the town are fictional characters.)

20.subject: The Nature of Love
20.title: He Paid Her $1,000 a Day to Love His Son
20.summary:
On his son's wedding day, Mr. Pembrook writes the bride a check. One thousand dollars. And another one tomorrow. And every single day after that. "My boy deserves a wife who adores him. So I bought him one."
Old Hattie, the gardener, keeps pruning: "Sir, you can't buy that."
"Hattie, I bought this house, this town, and the mayor's golf cart. Everything has a price." 💵

So every morning, an envelope. And every morning, Daisy smiles.
😂 She laughs at Theo's terrible jokes.
🍿 She holds his hand at the movies.
🤒 She sings to him when he's sick.
📅 Ten years. About $3.65 million.

Then one night, Theo finds the checkbook. He doesn't feel lucky. He feels robbed. Ten years of smiles, and he can't trust a single one.

You see, love that's bought isn't love, and neither is love that's forced.
🎭 A puppet can say "I love you" all day long, and it means nothing, because it can't say anything else.
🚪 Real love only exists where someone is free to say no, walk away, and break your heart.
❤️ That's why God gave us the power to rebel. He could have built puppets that never sin. He wanted children who could love Him back.

So Theo tears up the checkbook, opens the front door, and says, "You're free to go."
The next morning, the checks were gone. Daisy wasn't.

Could love ever be real if the other person had no choice? 👇
20.fiction_note: (Mr. Pembrook, Hattie, Theo and Daisy are fictional characters.)

21.subject: Innocent Suffering
21.title: Why Do Innocent Children Suffer? Follow the Dominoes
21.summary:
Talk-show host Rex Calloway slams his fist on the desk: "Show me one starving child, and I'll show you there's no good God. Case closed." The audience roars. 📺

In the front row, an old woman raises her hand. Ruth. Forty years as a children's nurse. "May I borrow your desk?"
She stands up a single domino. Then another. And another.

🍾 "This one is a father who chose the bottle." She taps it. Down they go, off the desk, out the door, across the city, all the way to a hospital, where a baby is born shaking.
⚔️ "This one is a general who chose a war." Click. A thousand miles of dominoes later, a little girl's bowl stays empty.

Nobody is laughing now.
"I won't make their pain small, Rex. But most of the time, children don't suffer for what they chose. They suffer for what we chose."

🔗 God made us free, and in a world this connected, our choices land on other people. Especially the little ones.
🌅 But the row doesn't end at the bottom. Jesus said, "Let the little children come to me." The Bible promises a day when God wipes every tear from their eyes, and every wrong done to them is answered.

Ruth picks up the last fallen domino and stands it back up.
"Their suffering is real, Rex. It just doesn't get the last word."

Where have you seen one person's choice fall on someone smaller? 👇

22.subject: Secular Ideology
22.title: He Tore Down Every Guardrail  Then the Fog Rolled In
22.summary:
The new county engineer tears down every guardrail on Dead Man's Curve. "Look at these cars. Airbags. Lane assist. Smart brakes. We've outgrown rusty old rails." The council applauds. Somebody cuts a ribbon. ✂️

Old Gus, who has patched that road for forty years, shakes his head. "Son, those rails were never about the cars."
"Gus, it's the twenty-first century. Nobody needs a fence to stay on the road."

That's the big promise today: drop the old religion, and humanity will naturally grow kinder. But history already ran that experiment.
🎓 The twentieth century was the most educated, most scientific century the world had ever seen, and the bloodiest.
⛪ In the Soviet Union, in China and in Cambodia, regimes that officially banished God tore down churches, burned scriptures, and declared the State the final judge of right and wrong.
🕯️ They didn't build paradise. Historians estimate tens of millions of their own people died.

🛡️ You see, a guardrail doesn't make you a good driver. It catches you when you're not. Remove the Lawgiver above the rulers, and nothing stands between a ruler and his worst idea.

That night, the fog rolls in. The engineer takes Dead Man's Curve a little too fast. His car stops six inches from the edge, against the one rail Gus never took down.

What do you think actually holds a powerful person back? 👇
22.fiction_note: (The engineer, Gus and the town are fictional characters.)
22.script:
The new county engineer tore down every guardrail on Dead Man's Curve.
"Look at these cars," he told the town. "Airbags. Lane assist. Smart brakes. We've outgrown rusty old rails."
The council applauded. Somebody cut a ribbon.
Old Gus, who had patched that road for forty years, just shook his head. "Son, those rails were never about the cars."
"Gus, it's the twenty-first century. Nobody needs a fence to stay on the road."
That's the big promise today. Drop the old religion, and humanity will naturally grow kinder.
But history already ran that experiment.
The twentieth century was the most educated, most scientific century the world had ever seen. And it was the bloodiest. In the Soviet Union, in China, in Cambodia, regimes that officially banished God tore down churches, burned scriptures, and declared the State the final judge of right and wrong.
They didn't build paradise. Historians estimate tens of millions of their own people died.
You see, a guardrail doesn't make you a good driver. It catches you when you're not. Remove the Lawgiver above the rulers, and nothing stands between a ruler and his worst idea.
That night, the fog rolled in. The engineer took Dead Man's Curve a little too fast.
His car stopped six inches from the edge.
Against the one rail Gus never took down.
